dialogReference.para: DTM: the bare-ground surface, predicted by machine learning; use it for fault mapping. DSM: the top of trees and buildings (five bands, about five times the data to stream).

Hillshade (lit from the chosen sun), slope in degrees (added switched off) and local relief model (LRM: height above or below the local mean, blue to red over +/- 2.5 m). Canopy check: green where the DSM is over 3 m above the DTM, i.e. where the DTM is the model's guess (streams the DSM too). Tile edges: outlines of the tiles, where seams may be.

Each pixel's height minus the mean height within this distance. Smaller radii show narrow features: 150 m for offset channels and narrow scarps, 300 m for scarps tens of metres wide, 1000 m for broad scarps and fold scarps (slow when live).
Area to cover. Leave blank for the current map view.
Automatic: a mosaic dataset with a Standard or Advanced licence, a VRT file with Basic. A mosaic dataset is quicker to draw; a VRT file is one small file that works with any licence.

Leave blank so tiles in one UTM zone keep their own 15 m grid. Across zones the tool picks GDA2020 / GA LCC (Australia), NZTM2000 (New Zealand) or a projection centred on your area. Choose a projected system in metres, never degrees.

Multidirectional lights the surface from several directions, so no scarp orientation is hidden. A single sun, or one shining across a fault trend, gives scarps facing it up to three times the contrast.
Direction the sun shines from, in degrees clockwise from north (for a single sun). 315 (north-west) is usual.

Trend of the fault you are mapping, in degrees (either direction along it, e.g. 30 for a NNE-SSW fault). The sun is put at right angles to it, on the side nearer north-west, so relief does not look inverted.
Height of the sun above the horizon, in degrees. A low sun brings out low scarps: about 20 on plains, 30-35 in steep country.
Vertical exaggeration of the hillshade. 1 shows true relief; 2-3 brings out subtle scarps on Australian plains, along with the DTM's noise.
The elevation source, tile edges and layer files written.

summary.para: Add GEM-15 elevation for the current map view in one step: a live hillshade and local relief model in a group, and the tile edges. Zoom to your area and press Run; nothing is downloaded beyond what is drawn.

usage.bullet_item: Works for views up to 6 x 6 degrees; use Add GEM-15 for Extent for more.
With a Standard or Advanced licence the elevation is a mosaic dataset; with Basic, a VRT file. Both stream from Google's public bucket; no account needed.
The local relief model is drawn at 1:50,000 and closer: zoom in to see it.

The DTM is predicted by machine learning: unreliable under trees and buildings (the canopy check shows where). Straight features along tile edges may be seams, not scarps. Heights are on the EGM96 geoid, not AHD.
